messages.author: 15e23bc7efd9579a
messages.subject: Vectorizing code
parts:
Hi there,

I wondered if there is any way I can vectorize my Stan code. I have written the following julia notebook which explains and implements a model for estimation the proportion non-null z-scores, to be used in multiple testing problems.

I would ideally use the model on GWAS summary stats which contains more than 100k data points (if not ~1M), and would like to know if my current implementation can be improved.

https://dl.dropboxusercontent.com/u/483049/enrichment.html

Is there any thing I can do to speed up my code?

Any help is highly appreciated.

Best
Jon Alm Eriksen

messages.author: 15e23bc7efd9579a
messages.subject: Re: Vectorizing code
parts:
Apparently, public dropbox folders does no longer render html files,
so here is the code in question.

data {
int<lower=0>  K;  // # of covariates
int<lower=0>  N0; // # of z-scores with abs(z) < xi
int<lower=0>  N1; // # of z-scores with abs(z) >= xi
real<lower=0> xi; // threshold for abs(z)
real<lower=0> A;  // sum of z^2 for z-scores with abs(z) < xi
matrix[N0,K]  C0; // Covariate matrix for the z-scores with abs(z) < xi
matrix[N1,K]  C1; // Covariate matrix for the z-scores with abs(z) >= xi
}
parameters {
real<lower=0> sigma; // standard deviation null distribution
real<lower=0,upper=1> thetatilde; // mean proportion of non null z-scores
vector[K] alpha; // covariate coefficients
}
model {
real V; // Mass of null distribution with abs(z)>xi
vector[N0] theta0;
vector[N1] theta1;

// Priors
sigma ~ gamma(3,2); // mean=3/2, mode=(3-1)/2=1
thetatilde ~ beta(1,1); // flat
for (i in 1:K)
    alpha[i] ~ cauchy(0,5);

// Intermediate
V = 2*normal_cdf(-xi, 0, sigma);
theta0 = logit(thetatilde)+ C0*alpha;
theta1 = logit(thetatilde)+ C1*alpha;

// Model
for (i in 1:N0)
    target += log(1 - inv_logit(theta0[i]));

for (i in 1:N1)
    target += log(inv_logit(theta1[i]) * (1.0 - V) + V);

target +=  - N0*log(sigma) - 0.5*A*pow(sigma,-2);
}

Is there any way I can vectorize this, and avoid traversing all the
data with for loops, or speed it up by other means?

Best
Jon

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Vectorizing code
parts:
> On Oct 10, 2016, at 4:26 PM, Jon Alm Eriksen <jon.alm...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
> Apparently, public dropbox folders does no longer render html files,
> so here is the code in question.
>
> data {
> int<lower=0> K; // # of covariates
> int<lower=0> N0; // # of z-scores with abs(z) < xi
> int<lower=0> N1; // # of z-scores with abs(z) >= xi
> real<lower=0> xi; // threshold for abs(z)
> real<lower=0> A; // sum of z^2 for z-scores with abs(z) < xi
> matrix[N0,K] C0; // Covariate matrix for the z-scores with abs(z) < xi
> matrix[N1,K] C1; // Covariate matrix for the z-scores with abs(z) >= xi
> }
> parameters {
> real<lower=0> sigma; // standard deviation null distribution
> real<lower=0,upper=1> thetatilde; // mean proportion of non null z-scores
> vector[K] alpha; // covariate coefficients
> }
> model {
> real V; // Mass of null distribution with abs(z)>xi
> vector[N0] theta0;
> vector[N1] theta1;
>
> // Priors
> sigma ~ gamma(3,2); // mean=3/2, mode=(3-1)/2=1
> thetatilde ~ beta(1,1); // flat

You can drop the beta(1, 1) as it's just uniform
and that's the default --- uniform over values satisfying
the declared constraints.

>
> // Intermediate
> V = 2*normal_cdf(-xi, 0, sigma);
> theta0 = logit(thetatilde)+ C0*alpha;
> theta1 = logit(thetatilde)+ C1*alpha;
>
> // Model
> for (i in 1:N0)
> target += log(1 - inv_logit(theta0[i]));

>
> for (i in 1:N1)
> target += log(inv_logit(theta1[i]) * (1.0 - V) + V);

I don't understand why you're doing this, but it'd probably
be faster to use our bernoulli_logit with vectorization.

It'd be faster to code this as:

{
vector[N1] theta;

for (n in 1:N1)
theta[i] = inv_logit(theta1[i]);

theta = theta * (1 - V) + V;

1 ~ bernoulli(theta);
}

The braces give you a local scope in which to define theta.

It's more efficient to use our built-in normal distributions
and betnoulli_logit than trying to do this all yourself.

In transformed data,
define

halfA = -0.5 * A;

and then use

target += halfA / square(sigma) - N0 * log(sigma);

though that's unlikely to be a bottleneck.

- Bob

Jon
